Situation1: They send an occasional text to check in with their parents over the weekend.
Expectation2: Listen actively and provide emotional support when needed.
Situation2: A friend sends a text message complaining about having a long, boring day.
Story: It’s Saturday afternoon, and I’m curled up on the couch, scrolling through my phone. I see a message from Mom: “Hope you’re having a good weekend! Miss you.” I know she expects me to reply, maybe even call, just to check in and let her know I’m okay. I haven’t talked to her since last Sunday, and guilt pricks at me. Before I can type a response, my phone buzzes again. This time, it’s my friend, Jess: “Ugh, today sucked. Can I vent?” I know what she needs—someone to listen, to be there for her, to make her feel less alone. I stare at both messages, feeling the weight of their expectations. My mom wants reassurance and connection, Jess needs comfort and support. I want to be there for both, but I can already feel the tension rising in my chest, the pressure to not let either of them down. My fingers hover over the screen, torn between being a good daughter and a good friend, not sure which message to answer first.
